newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't sees "gentle" growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't sees "gentle" growth in 1997.

text.p: Brazil will see "gentle" economic growth throughout 1997 with savings and investment replacing consumption as the driving forces of the economy, a senior Finance Minsitry official said.
"What we expect for 1997 is gentle growth," the ministry's Economic Policy Secretary Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros told reporters after announcing a trade deficit of $853 million for November.

Information from the banking sector showed higher-than-usual levels of cash going into savings accounts, a sign that Brazilians were "more cautious" than in recent years regarding spending, Mendonca de Barros said.

Furthermore, importers appeared to have overestimated Christmas demand -- October's trade deficit was $1.3 billion -- and would not need to replenish their stocks after the holidays, a seasonal factor boosting first quarter output, he said.
"This year will be completely different to the frenzy of buying seen in 1994," Mendonca de Barros said.
A consumer boom in late 1994 spurred economic growth of 10 percent in the first quarter of 1995 and led the government to cool the economy with higher interest rates and credit restrictions.
Mendonca de Barros said the government saw no need to put on the brakes again and said investment would play a bigger role in growth.

Foreign direct investment in the year to December 10 jumped to $8.0 billion from $4.5 billion in 1995. That, plus upcoming privatizations and expansion in industry would bolster internal production and ease the trade deficit, the official said.
The government would meet its target of keeping the current account deficit to within three percent of gross domestic product this year and would do likewise in 1997, he said.
